B-trees:
- Definition: self-balancing tree data structure, maintains sorted data, allows search, sequential access, insertions, deletions in O(log n). B-tree is a generalization of binary search tree, nodes can have more than two children, each node contains keys and pointers. B-tree of order m: each node has at most m children, at least ceil(m/2) children except root, keys sorted. All leaves at same depth. B+ tree variant: data only in leaves, internal nodes for routing, linked leaves for sequential access.
- How works: Search: start root, compare keys, descend to appropriate child. Insert: find leaf, insert key, if overflow split node, propagate split upward. Delete: find key, if internal replace with predecessor/successor, if underflow borrow or merge. Maintains balance.
- Time complexity: Search O(log n) (base m? Actually height O(log_m n), but comparisons O(log n) if m constant? More precisely O(log n) with base m, but since m constant, O(log n). Insert/delete O(log n). Space O(n). For B+ tree, range queries O(log n + k) where k number of results.
- When choose over alternatives: B-trees vs binary search trees (AVL, red-black): B-trees reduce disk I/O because nodes are large, fit disk pages, high branching factor. Good for databases, file systems. B+ trees for range queries. Alternatives: hash tables for exact match O(1) but no range; skip lists for concurrent; LSM trees for write-heavy. B-trees for balanced, sorted, disk-based.
- Concrete examples: databases (MySQL InnoDB uses B+ tree), PostgreSQL, SQLite, filesystems (NTFS, ext4, HFS+), key-value stores (BoltDB, LMDB), indexes.
